overview: The exact atlas id Nejd covers two related but interrupted Saudi states: the First centered at Diriyah from 1744 to 1818, and the Second centered at Riyadh from 1824 to 1891. The six-year gap matters. Egyptian-Ottoman forces destroyed Diriyah; later Saudi rulers rebuilt power from another capital. Authority depended on oasis towns, tribal alliances, religious scholars, tribute, trade, and force, never a uniformly administered colored patch. Families farmed dates and grain, herded animals, copied books, traded, crafted textiles and weapons, hosted guests, and gathered for poetry and news. Women worked in households, markets, education, charity, and production, although official heritage sources preserve their lives unevenly. Wells, irrigation, baths, and high toilet towers appear in documented architecture. Period medical evidence is thin, so the card marks that gap instead of inventing a hospital system. Written-language sample: كتاب التوحيد, Kitab al-Tawhid, means Book of Monotheism. The atlas uses one unchanged polygon in 1783, 1800, and 1815, crosses the 1818 collapse, excludes major conquests, and vanishes before the 1891 ending.

periods.title: 1744 to 1765: alliance at Diriyah and a growing local state
periods.summary: Muhammad ibn Saud and Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab formed their political and religious alliance at Diriyah in 1744. The emir supplied protection and force; the scholar supplied a reform program and scholarly network. Expansion began among the rival oasis settlements of central Najd rather than across an empty desert.

periods.title: 1765 to 1792: consolidation in Najd and caravan connections
periods.summary: Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad succeeded in 1765 and extended authority across more Najdi towns. Diriyah remained a mixed settlement of farmers, merchants, artisans, minor scholars, and enslaved people. Limited local surpluses in dates and livestock made caravan trade toward al-Ahsa, Basra, and India economically important.

periods.title: 1792 to 1804: eastern expansion, Karbala, and the Hijaz
periods.summary: After Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab died in 1792, the state expanded into al-Ahsa and toward the Gulf. Saudi forces raided Karbala in 1801 and took Mecca in 1802; Medina followed by 1804. Firearms, caravan imports, mobile levies, and coercion helped turn a Najdi coalition into regional power.

periods.title: 1804 to 1818: Hajj rule, imperial war, and Diriyahs destruction
periods.summary: Imam Saud supervised the Hajj during seven seasons, while his policies and control of the holy cities provoked broad opposition. Ottoman Sultan Mahmud II relied on Muhammad Ali of Egypt to reconquer western and central Arabia. Ibrahim Pashas forces besieged Diriyah and destroyed the capital in 1818.

periods.title: 1818 to 1824: occupation and a real break between states
periods.summary: After Diriyah fell, Abdullah ibn Saud was taken to Istanbul and executed. Egyptian-Ottoman garrisons and local rivals contested central Arabia, while surviving Saudi family members attempted restorations. This interval was not a quieter chapter of one continuous government; the First State had ended and the Second did not exist yet.

periods.title: 1824 to 1843: Turki restores rule from Riyadh
periods.summary: Turki ibn Abdullah expelled remaining Egyptian authority from Riyadh in 1824 and made it the new Saudi capital. His assassination in 1834 brought Faisal ibn Turki to power. Egyptian forces returned, captured Faisal in 1838, and installed rivals before he escaped and recovered Riyadh in 1843.

periods.title: 1843 to 1865: Faisals restored rule and negotiated reach
periods.summary: Faisal ibn Turki ruled from Riyadh for a long second reign, collecting tribute and balancing oasis towns, tribes, Gulf neighbors, Egypt, and Ottoman claims. Lewis Pellys 1865 visit shows a court engaged with foreign envoys and geographic intelligence. Faisals authority remained negotiated and varied greatly beyond the capital.

periods.title: 1865 to 1891: succession war, Ottoman al-Ahsa, and Rashidi victory
periods.summary: Faisals death triggered rivalry among his sons Abdullah, Saud, and Abd al-Rahman. Abdullah sought Ottoman help; Ottoman forces occupied al-Ahsa in 1871, while Al Rashid power grew from Hail. Muhammad ibn Rashid defeated the Saudis decisively at al-Mulayda in 1891, ending their Riyadh state and driving the family toward exile.

sections.title: Read the name, dates, and map with caution

items.text: The exact software id is nejd, indexed as Nejd from 1783 to 1878. Its summary describes the timeless geographic region, but coverage classifies the record as a state. No reviewed card, override, or staged draft existed. This packet narrows it to the First and Second Saudi States in Najd.

All fifty border snapshots were decoded. The exact id occurs in 1783, 1800, and 1815, always as one Polygon with one component, one ring, and eighteen positions. Every coordinate is identical, so three date labels do not provide three independent reconstructions of changing Saudi authority.

The polygon includes sampled Diriyah, Riyadh, Uyayna, Huraymila, Shaqra, Dawadmi, al-Kharj, and Wadi al-Dawasir. It excludes Buraydah, Unayzah, Hail, Hofuf, Qatif, Mecca, Medina, Taif, Jeddah, and Karbala, including places the First State historically conquered or raided beyond its Najdi core.

Each target snapshot shares exactly two TopoJSON arcs with the Ottoman Empire layer, yet no tested point has overlapping owners and no polygonal overlap candidate appears. Shared drawing seams can reveal atlas assembly, but they do not prove a surveyed treaty frontier or continuous Ottoman administration inside central Najd.

The layer appears after 1715, remains geometrically frozen through 1815, and disappears at the 1878 snapshot while the Second Saudi State continued until 1891. In 1878 and 1900 the sampled interior becomes generic Arabia; a different Arabia Nejd record appears later. These are software seams, not political birthdays or funerals.

sections.title: Build a state through alliance, preaching, and force

items.text: The 1744 Diriyah alliance joined Muhammad ibn Sauds political project to Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhabs campaign against practices he considered unlawful innovations. The partnership proved durable, but Najdi scholars did not speak with one voice. His own relatives and other learned opponents challenged teachings that later state narratives present as inevitable.

Diriyah was no glittering imperial capital at the start. It was an oasis settlement of farmers, small merchants, artisans, minor religious scholars, and enslaved residents. Its limited dates and livestock could not support expansion alone, which is why outside trade, tribute, alliances, and military extraction mattered so much.

Saudi campaigns mobilized different mixtures of town levies, tribal allies, camel-riding infantry, and horsemen. Matchlocks became especially important for foot soldiers, and commanders might demand able-bodied men who owned riding camels. These forces were coalitions, not a modern standing army wearing identical uniforms and waiting for payroll.

Taking Mecca and Medina made pilgrimage administration an international political issue. Imam Saud personally supervised Hajj seasons and changed practices at the holy places; many Muslims opposed those measures. Control of pilgrimage routes offered prestige and revenue, but it also helped provoke the imperial campaign that eventually reached Diriyah.

The alliance survived the destruction of its capital because religious teaching had spread through settled communities and family networks. The Library of Congress history stresses that political authority collapsed in 1818 while the reform remained rooted in southern Najd and Jabal Shammar. Ideas proved harder to demolish than mud-brick walls.

sections.title: Expand, trade, and endure the First States violent ending

items.text: Najd was connected to wider markets long before oil. Caravans carried dates, camels, sheep, and horses outward and brought guns, metal parts, cloth, and other goods inward through al-Ahsa, Basra, and Gulf ports. The imported matchlock is a useful antidote to the cartoon of an entirely isolated desert interior.

The First States reach varied by place and season. QDL records describe authority in the Gulf and Trucial Oman as changing with the effective force available. A tribute payment, appointed agent, raid, or temporary submission did not automatically create the same everyday government that residents experienced in Diriyah.

At-Turaif became the political center of the Saudi dynasty on the edge of Diriyahs oasis. Palaces, mosques, houses, walls, and administrative spaces grew together in a distinctive Najdi earthen style. The architecture shows concentrated resources and skilled labor, while its ruins also record bombardment, abandonment, and later weathering.

The state took al-Ahsa, Mecca, and Medina and raided Karbala, yet the atlas polygon excludes every sampled site. That mismatch is instructive: expansion consisted of conquests, garrisons, alliances, tribute, and contested routes, not a stable filled shape. A campaign arrow and a household tax collector describe different kinds of power.

Ibrahim Pashas army reached Diriyah after a long campaign supplied from Egypt and the Hijaz. Siege warfare damaged houses, walls, palm groves, and irrigation, making civilians pay through hunger and lost livelihoods. In 1818 the capital surrendered and was destroyed; this was a state ending, not a tidy map update.

sections.title: Restore rule from Riyadh, then lose it to civil war

items.text: Turki ibn Abdullah restored Saudi rule from Riyadh in 1824, six years after Diriyahs fall. A new capital, altered territorial reach, and different external constraints justify calling this the Second Saudi State. The same ruling family and religious partnership provided continuity, but continuity does not erase institutional collapse and re-creation.

Faisal ibn Turki was captured during renewed Egyptian intervention, spent years away, and returned to power in 1843. His second reign required bargaining with town leaders, tribes, neighboring rulers, and larger empires. Restoration was less like flipping a palace switch and more like repeatedly persuading armed partners that cooperation paid.

Lewis Pelly reached Riyadh in 1865 seeking political intelligence and a meeting with Faisal. His notes preserve geography and court contact, but they also reflect a British imperial observer gathering strategic information. The journey is useful evidence precisely when read as an interested mission, not a neutral neighborhood tour.

Faisals death opened a succession struggle among his sons. A Najdi judge facing rival claimants, civil war, and foreign intervention had to decide what legitimate obedience meant in practice. Scholarly law was not floating above politics; rulings could shape alliances, reputations, taxes, safety, and whether another army entered town.

Muhammad ibn Rashid built a powerful rival state from Hail and worked with Ottoman authorities. Rashidi victory was therefore neither a random tribal ambush nor simple Ottoman annexation. By 1891 a regional coalition centered on Hail had beaten the Riyadh Saudis, while imperial partnership strengthened the winners without eliminating local agency.

sections.title: Live in families, neighborhoods, farms, and moving camps

items.text: Official heritage research describes households that could include spouses, children, grandchildren, and sometimes married grandchildren under one roof. Work divided by gender but overlapped in agriculture, herding, cooking, cleaning, and child care. That pattern varied by wealth, place, season, enslavement, and whether a family was settled or mobile.

Pastoral families followed rainfall and water toward grazing, then visited towns to sell ghee or livestock and buy wheat and dates. Evenings could bring fire, poetry, and exchanged news. The desert version of refreshing your feed required another traveler, a good memory, and preferably a camel that had stopped complaining.

Women in Diriyah produced food, preserved dates, made dairy products and spices, raised animals, sewed clothing, and sold goods. Some kept small home shops or worked as traveling sellers. The source is a modern state heritage synthesis, so its named examples are valuable while its celebratory framing deserves visible caution.

Some women taught, copied or practiced calligraphy, endowed books, composed poetry, and offered protection or charity. Fatima al-Fadaili reportedly held scholarly authorization to teach, while Jawhara bint Faisal endowed books. Such cases disprove total female absence from learning without proving equal access for every girl or social class.

Food preparation was skilled household labor: wheat, jareesh, rice, bread, asida, meat, thareed, dairy, dates, pepper, and dried lime all appear in heritage accounts. Recipes changed with income, harvest, trade, and scarcity. A ruler might announce a campaign, but somebody still had to grind grain before breakfast.

sections.title: Build with mud, manage water, and answer the toilet question

items.text: Najdi builders set mud-brick or plastered walls on stone courses, spanned roofs with tamarisk beams and palm matting, and used internal courtyards for light and circulation. Many houses had two storeys and roof living space. These materials were locally intelligent, but rain, neglect, and artillery were brutally effective maintenance inspectors.

A typical Najdi house turned inward through an indirect entrance toward a courtyard. Sleeping, eating, sitting, and storage rooms clustered around it; a separate stair could lead guests to an upper majlis while a family stair preserved household circulation. Attached walls made neighboring homes look almost continuous from outside.

Wadi Hanifahs shallow water table supported Diriyahs oasis. People drew well water, sometimes using donkeys or camels, while gardens and palms depended on repeated lifting and distribution. The grand palaces make good photographs, but the animals walking circles at a well helped keep the capital alive one bucket at a time.

Yes, the toilet evidence exists: UNESCO records high toilet towers among distinctive early Najdi architectural features at At-Turaif. The source does not establish that every home had one, how waste was removed, or whether rural camps used comparable arrangements. A tower is documented; a universal sewer system definitely is not.

Al-Ahsa, controlled by the Saudi states during some phases, joined springs, wells, canals, gardens, settlements, markets, and drainage. Traditional systems moved shallow groundwater by gravity or lifting devices across small plots. Water management produced dates and other crops, but control of the oasis repeatedly attracted rival states for exactly that reason.

sections.title: Farm, herd, trade, craft, and handle dangerous technology

items.text: Most early Diriyah residents depended on farming, small commerce, craft, or livestock rather than court employment. Dates and animals supplied only modest surpluses, so merchants traveled to al-Ahsa, Basra, and India. Political expansion did not spring from limitless oasis wealth; it drew resources from widening trade and tribute networks.

Imported matchlocks were transformative technology. Thousands of guns or gun parts likely entered Najd through caravan trade before the great conquests, while stories that Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab personally taught local gunmaking lack credible support. The fun version is memorable; the sourced version gives merchants and repairers their due.

Al-Ahsas date landscape combined millions of palms, other crops, historic souqs, houses, mosques, wells, canals, and drainage. The modern UNESCO count cannot be projected backward as an eighteenth-century statistic, but the enduring system shows why eastern oases mattered as food producers, market centers, and gateways to Gulf trade.

Diriyahs al-Mawsim market served townspeople, caravans, and pastoral visitors selling camels, sheep, and ghee. Heritage sources describe spaces or times for women and men, alongside jewelry, weapons, cloth, and clothing. A market also hosted lessons, proving that shopping, gossip, livestock, and scholarship could share an address.

Nineteenth-century Najd faced outward toward Iraq as well as the Gulf. Political frontiers did not seal caravan routes, scholars, pilgrims, correspondence, or imported goods. That wider orientation helps explain why events in Basra, Baghdad, al-Ahsa, Kuwait, Egypt, and Istanbul repeatedly entered Riyadh politics and ordinary household prices.

sections.title: Learn, copy books, debate, and read a written sample

items.text: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab studied with scholars linked to the Hijaz, Basra, al-Ahsa, and Damascus and received ijazas, authorizations to transmit or teach particular learning. His opponents also belonged to learned traditions. Education moved through teachers, travel, books, family lines, and debate, not through one centrally approved school syllabus.

Student endowments in Diriyah could provide teaching rooms, sleeping space, food, storage, a mosque, and stables. Katatib taught Quran, Arabic, reading, and writing, while mosque circles offered advanced lessons. These institutions document organized learning, though enrollment totals and equal access across gender and class remain uncertain.

Books were expensive objects made valuable by paper, ink, skilled copying, and transport. Najdi copyists often prioritized jurisprudence and religious works, while ownership notes and marginalia connected manuscripts to people and journeys. A library could fit in a chest, yet still represent years of labor and several caravan routes.

Learning reached beyond rulers and famous scholars through mosque lessons, private reading, memorization, copying, apprenticeships, and oral teaching. Surviving catalogs favor texts that owners preserved, especially law and religion. They reveal intellectual networks beautifully while saying much less about a farm childs first letters or a craftswomans calculations.

Written-language sample: كتاب التوحيد. Read right to left and romanized Kitab al-Tawhid, it means Book of Monotheism. Oxford identifies it as Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhabs best-known work, and the library catalog secures the Arabic title. This is a period-authored text sample, not reconstructed casual conversation.

sections.title: Face illness, healing, hunger, and the archives silence

items.text: The reviewed period sources do not document a state hospital, health ministry, vaccination program, or standardized medical service in Najd before 1891. A later health history places organized public institutions in the twentieth century. That absence is evidence about government capacity, not proof that sick people received no care.

Later Saudi medical history records households and local healers using Quranic recitation, herbs or teas, cautery, and cupping in the early twentieth century. Some practices may have older roots, but this card will not paste them unchanged onto 1744. Continuity is plausible context; an exact eighteenth-century prescription requires exact evidence.

Period evidence is especially thin for childbirth, infant care, disability, dental pain, and womens healing work. Families, neighbors, midwives, scholars, and practical specialists almost certainly responded to illness, but the reviewed sources do not securely reconstruct their routines. The honest medical tidbit here is that the archive has a fever too.

War created health crises without needing a germ theory. Sieges cut food, damaged palms and irrigation, displaced households, and exposed civilians to injury and hunger. Destroying a date grove harmed many future meals, not just one battle. Military achievement and public suffering belong in the same paragraph.

Water and waste management were local architectural problems. Wells sustained the oasis, bath facilities served selected guests, and toilet towers existed at At-Turaif, but no reviewed source demonstrates a citywide sewer or universal sanitation service. Cleanliness depended on labor and access, while contamination risks remained largely unmeasured.

sections.title: Measure achievements, endings, and what continued

items.text: At-Turaifs achievement was a complete oasis capital rather than one photogenic palace: government, worship, homes, teaching, storage, reception, defense, water, and craft fit a terrain-adapted earthen city. UNESCO recognition also warns against triumphal certainty, because much survives as archaeology reconstructed through conservation choices and modern national memory.

The Saudi states linked dispersed Najdi towns and mobile groups into wider political projects, expanded caravan security in some phases, and supported a durable scholarly network. They also conquered, raided, coerced tribute, restricted rival religious practices, and suffered repeated revolt. Achievement becomes more meaningful when its human costs stay visible.

After 1865, fraternal civil war weakened Riyadh while Ottoman troops took al-Ahsa and Rashidi strength grew. The historical lesson is painfully domestic: a succession dispute inside one ruling family could invite foreign intervention, divide towns and tribes, redirect taxes, and turn yesterday’s allies into tomorrows siege planners.

Muhammad ibn Rashids forces defeated the Saudis at al-Mulayda in 1891. Riyadh then fell under Rashidi dominance, and Abd al-Rahman led the Al Saud family toward exile. The Second Saudi State dissolved, but Najdi farms, markets, families, mosques, books, and local authorities did not vanish with its court.

Abd al-Aziz ibn Abd al-Rahman recaptured Riyadh in 1902 and began a third Saudi state, later proclaimed the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932. That later success is connected family history, not a reason to stretch this card past 1891. Separate states deserve separate endings, especially after eleven years of Rashidi rule.

ending.text: In 1891, Muhammad ibn Rashids forces defeated the Riyadh Saudis at al-Mulayda and ended the Second Saudi State. Abd al-Rahman ibn Faisal and his family withdrew and eventually lived in Kuwait, while Rashidi governors dominated much of Najd. The ending was a political dissolution, not the disappearance of Najdi people, farms, tribes, towns, markets, scholars, books, or the Al Saud family. Abd al-Aziz recaptured Riyadh in 1902 and began a distinct third state. The atlas drops the exact nejd id in 1878, thirteen years too early, so that software seam must not be presented as the fall.
